board_asks: ray diagrams for mirrors & lenses, the mirror/lens formula numericals (with sign convention), refractive index, power of a lens, and the uses of concave / convex mirrors — the first four carry almost every mark here.

definitions.verbatim: (i) The angle of incidence is equal to the angle of reflection, and (ii) The incident ray, the normal to the mirror at the point of incidence and the reflected ray, all lie in the same plane.
definitions.plain: the ray comes in and bounces off at the same angle to the normal ($\angle i = \angle r$), and the incident ray, normal and reflected ray are all flat in one plane.

definitions.term: Laws of refraction of light (Snell's law)
definitions.verbatim: (i) The incident ray, the refracted ray and the normal to the interface of two transparent media at the point of incidence, all lie in the same plane. (ii) The ratio of sine of angle of incidence to the sine of angle of refraction is a constant, for the light of a given colour and for the given pair of media. This law is also known as Snell's law of refraction.
definitions.plain: $\dfrac{\sin i}{\sin r}$ stays the same for a given colour of light and a given pair of media — that constant is the refractive index.

definitions.verbatim: If medium 1 is vacuum or air, then the refractive index of medium 2 is considered with respect to vacuum. This is called the absolute refractive index of the medium.
definitions.plain: measured against vacuum/air, $n_m = \dfrac{\text{Speed of light in air}}{\text{Speed of light in the medium}} = \dfrac{c}{v}$ (NCERT p.149). A larger $n$ means light slows more — the medium is optically denser.

definitions.term: Principal focus & focal length of a spherical mirror
definitions.verbatim: [Rays parallel to the principal axis] are all meeting/intersecting at a point on the principal axis of the mirror. This point is called the principal focus of the concave mirror. … The distance between the pole and the principal focus of a spherical mirror is called the focal length.
definitions.plain: parallel rays converge at F (concave) — focal length $f$ = pole-to-F distance, and $R = 2f$.

definitions.term: Magnification produced by a spherical mirror
definitions.verbatim: Magnification produced by a spherical mirror gives the relative extent to which the image of an object is magnified with respect to the object size. It is expressed as the ratio of the height of the image to the height of the object.
definitions.plain: $m = \dfrac{h'}{h} = -\dfrac{v}{u}$. A negative $m$ means a real, inverted image; positive means virtual, erect.

definitions.term: Power of a lens & the dioptre
definitions.verbatim: The power of a lens is defined as the reciprocal of its focal length. … The SI unit of power of a lens is 'dioptre'. It is denoted by the letter D. … 1 dioptre is the power of a lens whose focal length is 1 metre. 1D = 1 m⁻¹.
definitions.plain: $P = \dfrac{1}{f\,(\text{metres})}$. Convex lens → positive power, concave → negative.

definitions.verbatim: The centre of the reflecting surface of a spherical mirror is a point called the pole."
…This point is called the centre of curvature of the spherical mirror."
The radius of the sphere of which the reflecting surface of a spherical mirror forms a part, is called the radius of curvature of the mirror."
[A straight line passing through the pole and the centre of curvature…] This line is called the principal axis."
The diameter of the reflecting surface of spherical mirror is called its aperture."
…the radius of curvature is found to be equal to twice the focal length. We put this as R = 2f."
A transparent material bound by two surfaces, of which one or both surfaces are spherical, forms a lens."
The central point of a lens is its optical centre. … A ray of light through the optical centre of a lens passes without suffering any deviation." (p.150–151)

concepts.title: Image formation by spherical mirrors
concepts.body: Trace two standard rays; where they meet is the image. The case below — object beyond C in a concave mirror — gives a real, inverted, diminished image.

concepts.title: Mirror formula & magnification
concepts.body: $\dfrac{1}{v} + \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{f}$ and $m = \dfrac{h'}{h} = -\dfrac{v}{u}$. Apply the sign convention before substituting.

concepts.title: Refraction & refractive index
concepts.body: Light bends toward the normal entering a denser medium. $n = \dfrac{c}{v} = \dfrac{\sin i}{\sin r}$.

concepts.title: Refraction through a glass slab & everyday refraction
concepts.body: Light bends when it crosses from one transparent medium into another because its speed changes — towards the normal going air → glass (rarer → denser), away from the normal going glass → air. In a rectangular slab the two bends are equal and opposite, so the emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray but shifted sideways. The same bending is why the bottom of a pond appears raised, a pencil partly in water looks displaced at the surface, and letters under a thick slab seem to rise — explain these qualitatively.
concepts.tested: 2-mark "explain why" · everyday-phenomenon; the glass-slab ray diagram (CBSE practical 11)

concepts.title: Applications of spherical mirrors and lenses
concepts.body: Concave mirrors give a powerful parallel beam when the source sits at the focus — torches, search-lights and vehicle headlights — and a large erect image when the object is within the focus, which is why they serve as shaving mirrors and dentists' mirrors; large ones concentrate sunlight to produce heat in solar furnaces. Convex mirrors are the rear-view (wing) mirrors of vehicles: the image is always erect (though diminished) and the outward curve gives a much wider field of view than a plane mirror. Lenses: a convex lens as a magnifying glass (watchmakers), spectacle lenses that correct defects of vision (concave for myopia, convex for hypermetropia — Ch 10), and lens combinations in cameras, microscopes and telescopes.
concepts.tested: 1–2 mark "name the type of mirror used in … and give a reason" (NCERT Exercise Q8: headlights, rear-view mirror, solar furnace)

source.note: uses of concave mirrors p.140; uses of convex mirrors p.142; magnifying glass and spectacle lenses p.150; lens combinations in cameras, microscopes and telescopes p.158

examples.problem_verbatim: An object, 4.0 cm in size, is placed at 25.0 cm in front of a concave mirror of focal length 15.0 cm. At what distance from the mirror should a screen be placed in order to obtain a sharp image? Find the nature and the size of the image.

solution_steps.text: $v = -37.5$ cm → the screen should be placed 37.5 cm in front of the mirror; the image is real.
$h' = -\dfrac{v\,h}{u} = -\dfrac{(-37.5)(4.0)}{(-25.0)} = -6.0$ cm → the image is inverted and enlarged.

examples.mark_logic: 1 for signed data, 1 for formula + solving $v$, 1 for nature + size with sign. Stating "real, inverted, enlarged" is where the last mark sits.

examples.problem_verbatim: A 2.0 cm tall object is placed perpendicular to the principal axis of a convex lens of focal length 10 cm. The distance of the object from the lens is 15 cm. Find the nature, position and size of the image. Also find its magnification.

solution_steps.text: $v = +30$ cm → image is 30 cm on the other side of the lens; real and inverted.
$m = \dfrac{v}{u} = \dfrac{30}{-15} = -2$; $\;h' = h\dfrac{v}{u} = -4.0$ cm → real, inverted, two times enlarged.

examples.mark_logic: 1 signs · 1 formula + solve · 1 nature/size. Lens magnification is $+v/u$ (no minus, unlike the mirror's $m=-v/u$).

strategies.text: Write down $u, v, f$ with signs before touching the formula. Most marks are lost at the sign step, not the algebra.
Use any two of the three standard rays; the image is where the reflected/refracted rays meet.
Convert $f$ to metres first, then $P=1/f$ in dioptres.

pitfalls.text: ✕Sign convention errors — the #1 lost mark. Object distance $u$ is always negative; concave $f$ negative, convex $f$ positive.
✕Mixing mirror and lens magnification — mirror $m=-v/u$, lens $m=+v/u$.
✕Forgetting to convert to metres for power — $P=1/f$ needs $f$ in metres, not cm.
✕Not stating the nature — a numerical answer needs "real/virtual, erect/inverted, magnified/diminished" for full marks.

formula_strip.label: Mirror formula
formula_strip.heading: Mirror Formula
formula_strip.tip: Write u, v, f WITH signs before substituting.

formula_strip.label: Lens formula
formula_strip.heading: Lens Formula
formula_strip.tip: The only change from the mirror formula is the minus sign; magnification differs too (mirror m = −v/u, lens m = v/u).

formula_strip.label: Magnification
formula_strip.heading: Magnification of Mirrors and Lenses
formula_strip.tip: Negative m means real and inverted, positive m virtual and erect.

formula_strip.label: Refractive index
formula_strip.tip: Absolute refractive index n ≥ 1; higher n means slower light.

formula_strip.label: Power of lens
formula_strip.math: $P = \dfrac{1}{f\,(\text{m})}$  (dioptre, D) · lenses in contact: $P = P_1 + P_2 + \dots$
formula_strip.heading: Power of a Lens (Dioptre)

formula_strip.label: Mirror relation
formula_strip.tip: For a spherical mirror of small aperture only.

formula_strip.label: Rules and signs at a glance
formula_strip.math:
(i) The object is always placed to the left of the mirror or lens, so light falls on it from the left.
(ii) All distances parallel to the principal axis are measured from the pole of the mirror (or the optical centre of the lens).
(iii) Distances to the right of the origin (along +x) are positive; distances to the left (along −x) are negative.
(iv) Distances above the principal axis (along +y) are positive.
(v) Distances below the principal axis (along −y) are negative.

Signs at a glance. Object distance $u$ is always negative.
Mirror: $f$ is negative for a concave mirror and positive for a convex mirror; $v$ is negative for a real image and positive for a virtual image; $m$ is negative for a real image and positive for a virtual image.
Lens: $f$ is positive for a convex lens and negative for a concave lens; $v$ is positive for a real image and negative for a virtual image; $m$ is negative for a real (inverted) image and positive for a virtual (erect) image.
formula_strip.heading: New Cartesian Sign Convention

formula_strip.label: Position of object → position, size and nature of image
formula_strip.math:
At infinity → at the focus F; highly diminished, point-sized; real and inverted
Beyond C → between F and C; diminished; real and inverted
At C → at C; same size; real and inverted
Between C and F → beyond C; enlarged; real and inverted
At F → at infinity; image would not be formed
Between P and F → behind the mirror; enlarged; virtual and erect
formula_strip.heading: Image Formation by a Concave Mirror (Table)

formula_strip.label: Position of object → position, size and nature of image
formula_strip.math:
At infinity → at the focus F, behind the mirror; highly diminished, point-sized; virtual and erect
Between infinity and the pole P → between P and F, behind the mirror; diminished; virtual and erect
formula_strip.heading: Image Formation by a Convex Mirror (Table)

formula_strip.label: Position of object → position, size and nature of image
formula_strip.math:
At infinity → at focus F₂; highly diminished, point-sized; real and inverted
Beyond 2F₁ → between F₂ and 2F₂; diminished; real and inverted
At 2F₁ → at 2F₂; same size; real and inverted
Between F₁ and 2F₁ → beyond 2F₂; enlarged; real and inverted
At focus F₁ → at infinity; image would not be formed
Between focus F₁ and optical centre O → on the same side of the lens as the object; enlarged; virtual and erect
formula_strip.heading: Image Formation by a Convex Lens (Table)

formula_strip.label: Position of object → position, size and nature of image
formula_strip.math:
At infinity → at focus F₁; highly diminished, point-sized; virtual and erect
Between infinity and optical centre O → between F₁ and O; diminished; virtual and erect
A concave lens always gives a virtual, erect and diminished image, whatever the position of the object.
formula_strip.heading: Image Formation by a Concave Lens (Table)

formula_strip.label: Laws of Refraction (Snell's Law)
formula_strip.math: (i) The incident ray, the refracted ray and the normal to the interface at the point of incidence all lie in the same plane. (ii) For light of a given colour and a given pair of media, $\dfrac{\sin i}{\sin r}=\text{constant}$ (Snell's law). Going from an optically rarer to an optically denser medium, light slows down and bends towards the normal; going from denser to rarer, it speeds up and bends away from the normal.

formula_strip.label: Laws of Reflection
formula_strip.math: (i) The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection. (ii) The incident ray, the reflected ray and the normal at the point of incidence all lie in the same plane. The image formed by a plane mirror is virtual, erect and the same size as the object.

formula_strip.label: Refraction through a Rectangular Glass Slab
formula_strip.math: For a rectangular glass slab the emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray, but it is displaced sideways (lateral displacement).

shortcuts.text: In every NCERT table: real image ⇒ inverted; virtual image ⇒ erect.
m negative ⇒ real, inverted. m positive ⇒ virtual, erect. A positive m of ½ with a mirror ⇒ convex mirror.
A convex mirror and a concave lens ALWAYS give a virtual, erect, diminished image.
Same-size image: concave mirror, object at C ⇒ image at C; convex lens, object at 2F₁ ⇒ image at 2F₂. In both, the image is real and inverted with m = −1.
Write the given values WITH signs (u −, f + or −) as the first line.
P = 1/f with f in METRES. Convex lens, f = +25 cm = +0.25 m ⇒ P = 1/(+0.25) = +4 D.
Object hamesha Left. Doori pole/centre se naapo. Right = Plus, Left = Minus, Upar = Plus, Neeche = Minus.
shortcuts.gloss: New Cartesian rules. Left → rule (i) object on the left; pole/centre se naapo → rule (ii); Right+/Left− → rule (iii); Upar+/Neeche− → rules (iv), (v).
shortcuts.heading: New Cartesian Sign Convention Trick

shortcuts.text: Convex mein Add (+), Concave mein Ghata (−), chahe mirror ho ya lens.
shortcuts.gloss: Sign of f. Convex mirror f +, convex lens f +; concave mirror f −, concave lens f − (NCERT sign convention).
Real inverted; virtual erect. R-U, V-S (matches all four tables).
Object positions in Table 9.1 order. A = At infinity · B = Beyond C · C = At C · B = Between C and F · F = At F · P = Between P and F.

shortcuts.text: Optically halka se optically bhaari: dheemi chaal, normal ki taraf. Optically bhaari se halka: tez chaal, normal se door.
shortcuts.gloss: Refraction bending (optical density = refractive index, not weight). optically rarer→denser: slows, bends towards normal; denser→rarer: speeds up, away.

third_tab_content.intro: CBSE does not require the mirror/lens formula derivation here — the formal core is the sign convention and ray rules that make every numerical and diagram correct.

rows.text: All distances measured from the pole / optical centre.
Distances against the incident light (object side) are negative.
Distances along the incident light are positive.
Object distance $u$ is always negative (real object).
Concave mirror / concave lens focal length: negative.
Convex mirror / convex lens focal length: positive.
